# The name Yama and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Yama** opens onto ​an entire world: the domain of death, justice, underworld, a Sanskrit tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name and ‌its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain that ‌makes the whole structure addressable. *yama* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Yama
- **ASCII form:** yama
- ​**Meaning:** "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead."
- **Domain of influence:** Death, Justice, Underworld
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** यम ​(Devanagari)

## Overview

**Yama** (*yama*) — Death, the First Mortal, Judge of the Dead · The god who presides over the Pitṛs — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under ​the domain "Death, Justice, Underworld". The name means "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead.".

**Yama** is death’s king in the Indian ​traditions: the first man to die, who found the way to the fathers’ world and now rules it — and judges who may enter. With his noose and his two four-eyed dogs, ​he waits at the southern direction, the realm of the ancestors, and his account-book is the oldest audit in human literature.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Yama** and serves its temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/yama/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *yama* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the ​restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **यम**. Etymologically it means "The god who presides over the ​Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead.".

The ASCII form *yama* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not ‌an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Yama** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed ​form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **y** → **Y** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Short /a/
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Short /a/

## The Original Script

The ‌name is preserved in Devanagari as **यम**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Yama*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Yama is written in Devanagari as यम
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel ​and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈjʌmə/** ‌— Sanskrit (IAST: Yama).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ya-** — Palatal y as in “young”; the a is short and open.
- **-ma** — The name means “twin” — Yama is the twin of ​Yamī in the earliest tradition.
- **Yam-** — In compound names the stem surfaces as yam- — the river Yamunā preserves his twin sister’s name.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ​“YUM-uh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Avestan** — Yima
- **Vedic** — Yamī (his twin sister)
- **Buddhist** — Yama/Enma

The lord of the dead was the first mortal — the one ​who found the path and guards it ever since.

## Mythology

Yama’s mythology moves from Vedic pathfinder to epic judge to Purāṇic king of hells. He begins as the twin who chose to ​die — the first of the race to walk the path — and becomes the stern accountant whose city the dead enter by the southern gate. Buddhism and the epics gave him ​his tortures and his buffalo; the Veda kept his dignity.

### The Twin Dialogue (Rigveda 10.10)

The oldest Yama-text is a dialogue: Yama and his twin Yamī, the first two beings, and Yamī’s ‌love for her brother. Yama refuses — ‘the immortals watch’ — and the hymn becomes the charter of exogamy and of the incest-taboo itself, argued between the world’s first twins in the world’s ​first debate.

### The Path of the Fathers (Rigveda 10.14)

The funeral hymn sends the dead king along the path Yama blazed, past the two dogs and the waters, to the feast of ‌the fathers where Yama waits with Varuṇa. ‘Leave the sin here, keep the glory’ — the formula of every Vedic funeral, spoken to the first traveller’s successor.

### The King Under the Earth ​(Mahābhārata)

In the epic’s underworld-book, Yama rules below with his city Saṃyamanī, his account read by Citragupta, his noose and his buffalo — the god of justice who once disguised himself as ‌a crab to test a king. The epic makes him dreaded and fair: the judge who cannot be bribed because he already owns everything.

### The Lord of the Narakas (Purāṇic Hell)

The ​Purāṇas enumerate eighty-four hells under Yama’s administration, each a precise torment for a precise sin — the liar’s tongue, the thief’s hands. Yet the same texts insist his justice is karma’s arithmetic, ‌not malice: even the tortures are purification, and release comes in time.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Yama concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement ​about the name:

- **The First Mortal** — He died before anyone — the twin who found the path to the fathers and became its king.
- **The Noose** — His pāśa, the noose, ‌finds every soul at its hour; none outrun it, though all may beg.
- **The Two Dogs** — Śyāma and Śabala, four-eyed, follow his road and report the dead; they guard the way.
- ​**Judge of the Deeds** — In the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas he reads the record of every soul — the karma, weighed without scales.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Yama survives ​in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

No Yama temples in the ‌Vedic sphere — the ancestor-cult needed no image. But his buffalo and noose carved into the doorposts of death-temples across Nepal and Bali, and the Enma iconography of Japanese temples from Kamakura ‌onward, mark the reach of his cult east.

## Realm & Domain

**Yama** is death’s king in the Indian traditions: the first man to die, who found the way to the fathers’ world ‌and now rules it — and judges who may enter. With his noose and his two four-eyed dogs, he waits at the southern direction, the realm of the ancestors, and his account-book ​is the oldest audit in human literature.

### The First Mortal

He died before anyone — the twin who found the path to the fathers and became its king.

### The Noose

His pāśa, ​the noose, finds every soul at its hour; none outrun it, though all may beg.

### The Two Dogs

Śyāma and Śabala, four-eyed, follow his road and report the dead; they guard the ‌way.

### Judge of the Deeds

In the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas he reads the record of every soul — the karma, weighed without scales.

## Across Cultures

The Avestan Yima, king of the golden ​age who kept death from his realm, is Yama’s Iranian twin — the same name, opposite function: where Yima postponed death, Yama administers it. Buddhism made Yama a dharmapāla, converted in the ​end by the Buddha’s teaching, and carried him east as Enma in Japan, where he still judges with his mirror and staff.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[hades|Hádēs]] (underworld ‌/ death), [[anubis|ꜣnpw]] (underworld / death), [[cerberus|Kérberos]] (underworld / death), [[ereshkigal|Ereškigal]] (underworld / death), [[forseti|Forseti]] (justice / law / truth), and [[garmr|Garmr]] (underworld / death).

## Cultural Legacy

Yama is the ancestor of ​every Asian judge-of-the-dead: Enma-ō in Japan, Yŏmna in Korea, Yanluo in China — a continuous iconography from the Veda to manga. The word ‘Yamī’ survives in the river Yamunā; and the maxim ​‘even Yama’s writ runs by karma’ structures the moral imagination of half the world’s population.

## The Scholarly Record

The account of Yama given in this edition rests on the witnesses and reference ‌works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

-  Rigveda 10.10 (the twin dialogue).
-  Rigveda 10.14 (the path ​to Yama).
-  Atharvaveda 18 (funerary hymns).
-  Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana & Vana Parvans.
-  Purāṇic Yama-cycle (Mārkaṇḍeya, Viṣṇu, Padma).

## A Meditation

Yama: the twin’s name, the first word of mortality. Restored plainly, it reads as ‌what it is — a name without ornament for the fact without ornament. Every other god in this lexicon borrows grandeur; Yama IS, which is why his name is the shortest sentence ​in Sanskrit.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored ​name is a small map. In the case of **Yama**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in ​the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *yama* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision ​is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the ‌drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **y**, **a**, **m**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what ​is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Yama in Its Tradition

**Yama** ​does not stand alone. It belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is counted among 102 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Death, Justice, Underworld — places it beside other ​figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When ‌the address bar shows **Yama**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. ​Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Yama** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Yama** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is ​not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can ‌paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened ​it to *yama*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. ‌That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, ‌each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Yama**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling ​used by this temple. The meaning "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead." anchors the name in its semantic field; without that ​anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Yama** and the ASCII form *yama* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization ​rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Yama aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is ​mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because ‌every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
